books.section: Topic 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Abraham Lincoln, Second Inaugural Address, March 4, 1865. Public domain. Wording verified against the Avalon Project and National Park Service texts. “. . .” marks omitted text between passages, quoted in their order in the source.
stimulus.text:
“One-eighth of the whole population were colored slaves, not distributed generally over the Union, but localized in the southern part of it. These slaves constituted a peculiar and powerful interest. All knew that this interest was somehow the cause of the war. . . . Yet, if God wills that it continue, until all the wealth piled by the bond-man’s 250 years of unrequited toil shall be sunk, and until every drop of blood drawn with the lash, shall be paid by another drawn with the sword, as was said 3,000 years ago, so still it must be said ‘the judgments of the Lord, are true and righteous altogether.’ . . . With malice toward none; with charity for all; . . . let us strive on to finish the work we are in; to bind up the nation’s wounds.”

—Abraham Lincoln, Second Inaugural Address, March 4, 1865

rationales.A: Background: in his First Inaugural Address Lincoln promised not to interfere with slavery where it already existed.
rationales.C: Background: in his First Inaugural Address Lincoln argued against secession and promised not to touch slavery in the states.
rationales.D: Background: in his First Inaugural Address Lincoln insisted the Union was unbroken and secession was illegal.
rationales.B: In 1861 Lincoln promised not to interfere with slavery where it existed, while in 1865 he named slavery as the cause of the war.
rationales.general:
1. Put the two speeches side by side: 1861 and 1865.
2. In 1861 Lincoln’s promise is restraint: he will not touch slavery where it exists.
3. In 1865 his claim is blame: slavery was somehow the cause of the war.
4. The war itself taught him to name the cause he once avoided.
Remember: a leader’s words change as the war teaches him what the war is about.
